list.listitem: Young athletes should be evaluated for previous concussion and incompletely healed prior injury. C

All competitive athletes should undergo a cardiovascular evaluation that includes personal history of exertion-related symptoms; family history of premature serious cardiac conditions and sudden death; the presence of heart murmur; and physical stigmata of Marfan syndrome. C
Recommendations for temporary or permanent sports disqualification should only be made when an athlete has probable or conclusive evidence of disease as opposed to those with borderline findings. C
Competitive athletes with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should be excluded from participating in most competitive sports except those of low intensity (see ). C
In female athletes, the presence of any of the following should prompt assessment for the presence of the others: hypomenorrhea or amenorrhea; disordered eating; and a history of stress fractures. C

background.definition: The pre-participation examination (PPE) is performed to promote safe participation in sports. The primary objectives of the PPE are to identify athletes at increased risk of sudden death or serious injury. A secondary goal is to conduct age-appropriate wellness care and to update immunizations. Pre-participation examinations are generally performed either by a single clinician or in groups where the athlete goes to multiple stations where multiple physicians and allied health professionals each perform a portion of the physical examination.

list.listitem: In the National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey, there were an average annual estimated 2.6 million emergency visits for sports-related injuries by persons between the ages of 5 and 24 years.
Male patients had 48 emergency department visits for sports injury per 1000 persons per year compared with 19 for female patients.

The rate of fatalities (cardiac and non-cardiac) during high school sport ranges from 0 to 1.5 per 100,000 participants. Among fall sports, football is responsible for 97%; of direct fatalities, while wrestling is the most common cause of direct fatalities or catastrophic injuries in the winter sports. In spring sports, there were 28 direct fatalities or catastrophic injuries in baseball and 46 in track and field.

A systematic review found that rates of sudden cardiac death varied from 1 in 3000 to 1 in 917,000. Higher quality studies found rates between 1 in 40,000 and 1 in 80,000. Men, African-Americans, and basketball players appear to be at higher risk.
Over 7 million high school students participate in sports each year.
Sports-related injury accounts for over 20% of all injury-related visits to emergency departments.
Concussion represent about 9% of high school athletic injuries and 6% of collegiate athletic injuries.
Nearly all catastrophic injuries (fatal and non-fatal) occur in football.
Sports can be classified by their probability of contact/collision as well as their static (isometric) and dynamic (isotonic) intensity (see ).
Traumatic injuries, including concussion, occur primarily during collision and contact sports (see for classification).
In athletes, stress fractures are primarily caused by overtraining and low caloric intake.

The majority of cardiac deaths in young athletes are due to congenital or acquired cardiac malformations. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the single most common cause, accounting for about 1/3 of deaths. Other important causes of sudden death include long QT syndrome and Marfan syndrome.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has a significant genetic basis.

list.listitem: Virtually all bodies regulating youth participation in sport require a preparticipation examination. Nonetheless, their effectiveness in reducing cardiac sudden death or injury is essentially unevaluated.

AHA Consensus panel guidelines (2006) recommend that the medical history, verified by a parent, should assess symptoms of exercise intolerance (chest discomfort, syncope, or near-syncope, excessive exertional fatigue or dyspnea), prior heart murmur, and elevated systemic blood pressure. The family history, also verified by a parent, should include premature cardiac death (sudden and unexpected before the age of 50), disability due to heart disease in surviving relatives under the age of 50 years; and specific cardiac disorders such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome and Marfan syndrome.

The cardiovascular physical examination should measure blood pressure in the seated position, femoral arterial pulses to excluded aortic coarctation, and assessment for heart murmur while the patient is supine and standing (or with Valsalva maneuver) to identify murmurs associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Murmurs that increase in intensity with standing or with Valsalva should raise concern for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Evaluate each patient for stigmata Marfan syndrome. Suspect it in the long, gangly patient with hyperflexible joints, pectus excavatum, kyphosis, and a murmur.

The American College of Preventive Medicine guidelines (2013) also support a pre-participation exam using a standardized H&P form developed by the AHA as described above. This guideline recommends against ECG, echocardiography, or genetic testing to detect persons at risk for sudden cardiac death. This is echoed by the Interassociation Consensus Statement on Cardiovascular Care of College Student Athletes from the US NCAA (2016), although they acknowledge that for elite athletes at this level a screening ECG is often included in the standard evaluation.

In adults beginning an exercise program, one series found that among 1361 asymptomatic adults with a normal ECG (mean age 50 years, only 10% women) 10% had an abnormal exercise stress test ut only 12 (1%) were ultimately diagnosed with coronary artery disease.

A systematic review identified studies of the accuray of exercise (stress) ECG in asymptomatic healthy athletes. The prevalence of an abnormal test was 0.6% (range 0-29%) with LVH the most common finding (57%), but the positive predictive value was low.
Adding point of care ultrasound to ECG may reduce false positives but is not guideline recommended at this time and cost may be prohibitive for all but elite athletes.

A systematic review of 15 studies with 47,137 athletes found a 0.3% overall rate of potentially lethal cardiovascular disorders, and concluded that ECG was more sensitive and specific than physical examination or history.

When ECG is performed in athletes, either due to increased risk or as a screening test, guidelines recommend that the Seattle criteria are used to classify ECG findings as normal or abnormal:
Normal ECG findings: sinus bradycardia ≥30 bpm, sinus arrhythmia, ectopic atrial rhythm, junctional escape rhythm, first degree AV block with PR interval >200 ms, Mobitz Type 1 (Wenckebach) second degree AV block, incomplete RBBB, early repolarization, and convex ST segment elevation combined with T wave inversion in leads V1-4 in black or African athletes. Isolated QRS voltage criteira for LVH may also be normal, with the exception it occurring in the presence of left atrial enlargment, left axis deviation, ST segment depression, T-wave inversion, or pathological Q waves.
Abnormal ECG findings: T wave inversion, ST segment depression, pathologic Q waves, incomplete LBBB, intraventricular conduction delay, left axis deviation, left atrial enlargement, RV hypertrophy, ventricular pre-excitation, short or long QT interval, Brugada like ECG pattern, sinus bradycardia <30 bpm, atrial tachyarrhythmia, PVC, and ventricular arrhythmia.

In female athletes, the presence of any of the following should be assessed for the presence of the others: hypomenorrhea or amenorrhea; disordered eating; and a history of stress fractures. About 4% of female athletes have the full “female athletic triad” of disordered menstrual cycles, disordered eating, and osteoporosis. The female athlete triad is more common in sports that emphasize a lean body, such as gymnastics and endurance sports.

Although preparticipation assessment for head injury is widely recommended, there are no evidence-based guidelines and there are no data to guide what the minimum requirements should be. A consensus statement recommends evaluation for concussion before participation, but acknowledges that the accuracy of recall by athletes is poor.

For each athlete, assess his or her overall flexibility and strength. For athletes with prior injury, perform a targeted functional assessment to determine if the injury has adequately healed. The most common injuries include ankle sprains, knee injuries, and shoulder injuries. See the individual chapters for details on the evaluation of these injuries.
Recommendations for temporary or permanent sports disqualification should only be made when an athlete has probable or conclusive evidence of disease as opposed to those with borderline findings. C
Competitive athletes with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should be excluded from participating in most competitive sports except those of low intensity (see ). C
Athletes with Marfan syndrome should not participate in competitive sports except those that are low intensity and non-contact (see ). C

Female athletes suspected to have the female athlete triad should undergo further diagnostic evaluation and be referred for nutritional counseling. Those with disordered eating should also be referred to eating disorders programs. Those who do not adhere with therapy should be excluded from training and competition. C
Recommendations for the temporary or permanent sports disqualification should only be made when an athlete has probable or conclusive evidence of disease as opposed to those with borderline findings.
Competitive athletes with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should be excluded from participating in most competitive sports except those of low intensity.

Athletes with mitral valve prolapse with a history of arrhythmogenic syncope, supraventricular tachycardia (sustained or repetitive nonsustained), severe mitral insufficiency, ejection fraction less than 50%, prior embolic event or with a family history of mitral valve-related sudden death should be excluded from participating in most competitive sports except those of low intensity.
All other athletes with mitral valve prolapse can engage in all competitive sports.
Athletes with Marfan syndrome should not participate in competitive sports except those that are low intensity and non-contact.
Athletes with newly diagnosed hypertension can participate in competitive sports, but need treatment and follow-up.
Athletes with blood pressure above 160/100 should be restricted from sports with high static (isometric) demands such as gymnastics, weight lifting, and rowing.
In addition to cardiovascular assessment, athletes with Down syndrome should have x-rays to assess atlanto-axial stability.
Athletes missing one paired organ (one eye, one kidney, etc.) should be excluded from contact or collision sports.

Female athletes suspected to have the female athlete triad should undergo further diagnostic evaluation and be referred for nutritional counseling. Those with disordered eating should also be referred to eating disorders programs. Those who do not adhere with therapy should be excluded from training and competition.
